topicName: AOF (Append-Only File), Fsync Policies, and AOF Rewrites
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Mastering Redis Persistence: AOF, Fsync Policies, and AOF Rewrites"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Redis offers robust persistence options to ensure data is not lost upon server restarts. While RDB (Redis Database) takes point-in-time snapshots, the Append-Only File (AOF) logs every write operation received by the server. This tutorial explores how AOF works, how fsync policies balance durability and performance, and how AOF rewrites prevent log files from growing indefinitely."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"How AOF Works"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"When AOF is enabled, Redis appends every mutating command (such as SET, HSET, or LPUSH) to the end of the AOF file using the Redis protocol format. When Redis restarts, it rebuilds the dataset by replaying these commands sequentially."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Command Buffering: Commands are first written to an in-memory buffer before being flushed to disk."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Human-Readable Protocol: The log consists of raw RESP (Redis Serialization Protocol) commands, making it possible to inspect or even manually edit the log if necessary."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Configuring Fsync Policies"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"Simply writing to the operating system's page cache does not guarantee that data hits the physical disk immediately. The fsync system call forces the OS to flush data to persistent storage. Redis provides three distinct fsync configurations in the redis.conf file to manage the trade-off between safety and speed:"},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"appendfsync always"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"The 'always' policy calls fsync every time a new command is appended. This guarantees maximum data durability because no data is lost upon crash, but it severely limits write performance since Redis waits for disk I/O to complete."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"appendfsync everysec"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"The 'everysec' policy calls fsync once every second. This is the default and recommended setting. It provides a balanced approach, offering high performance while risking the loss of at most one second of data in the event of a disaster."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"appendfsync no"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"With the 'no' policy, Redis never explicitly calls fsync. It leaves the flushing schedule entirely up to the operating system (typically every 30 seconds). This yields the highest write throughput, but offers the least data safety."},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding AOF Rewrites"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"Because AOF logs every single write, the file size grows continuously. For example, if you run 'SET counter 1' followed by 'INCR counter' a million times, the AOF file will contain a million entries, even though the final state is just 'counter 4194304'."},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"To solve this, Redis implements background AOF rewrites (BGREWRITEAOF). The rewrite process generates a brand-new, minimal AOF file representing the current in-memory dataset without replaying historical intermediate commands."},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"How BGREWRITEAOF Works Under the Hood"},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Forking: Redis forks a child process using copy-on-write semantics. The parent process continues to handle client queries and write to the existing AOF buffer."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Building the State: The child process writes the current dataset state to a temporary AOF file."},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Buffering New Writes: While the child writes the new file, the parent buffers any incoming new commands in a secondary AOF rewrite buffer."},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Atomic Swap: Once the child finishes, it signals the parent. The parent appends the buffered commands to the temporary file and atomically renames it to replace the old AOF file."},{"order":23,"type":"subheading","text":"Automatic Rewrite Configuration"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can configure Redis to trigger AOF rewrites automatically based on size growth thresholds inside redis.conf:"},{"order":25,"type":"code","text":"auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100\nauto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb"},{"order":26,"type":"paragraph","text":"In this configuration, Redis automatically triggers a rewrite when the current AOF file size is double (100% larger than) the size of the file after the last rewrite, provided the file is at least 64 megabytes in size."},{"order":27,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":28,"type":"paragraph","text":"Combining AOF with the 'everysec' fsync policy provides an optimal balance of durability and speed for most enterprise applications. Coupled with automated AOF rewrites, Redis ensures your log files remain compact, performant, and reliable over long periods of uptime."}]
